rationale: Tests the four elements of negligence (duty, breach, causation, damage) which are foundational — and specifically the Bolam + Bolitho standard for breach.
Tests the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur — specifically that it shifts the evidential burden to the defendant without requiring the plaintiff to prove specific negligence.
Tests recall of CPA 2019 key facts — specifically that it replaced the 1986 Act and raised jurisdictional thresholds — which changed how consumer cases against doctors are managed.
Tests whether students understand that free medical services at government hospitals are generally excluded from CPA coverage — a practically important distinction.
Tests the legally valid ingredients of informed consent using a clinical vignette — applying the required elements to a real scenario.
Tests the MTP Act 2021 amendment on minor consent — an explicitly high-stakes examination fact highlighted in the SDL clinical pearl.
Tests knowledge of the ICMR 2017 guidelines as the operative Indian framework — avoiding confusion with international frameworks like Belmont or Helsinki.
Tests the CTRI registration requirement — the SDL clinical pearl states explicitly that registration must precede enrolment.
Tests the legal status of passive euthanasia in India post-Common Cause 2018, distinguishing it from active euthanasia (illegal) and the role of Advance Directives.
Tests the doctrine of double effect as applied to palliative care — distinguishing this from active euthanasia, an important distinction for clinical practice.
Tests the HIV Act 2017's specific prohibition on mandatory testing — the clinical pearl explicitly distinguishes opt-out from mandatory testing, a high-frequency examination point.
Tests the anti-discrimination provisions — a doctor refusing to treat an HIV-positive patient is a violation of the Act, an important professional responsibility.
Tests knowledge of the NHRC's enabling legislation and its limitation — it cannot try cases directly but can recommend compensation and direct state action.

Tests the duty to document accurately in cases of suspected family violence — the SDL clinical pearl is explicit that fabricating a consistent history to protect a patient is itself a documentation violation.
Tests the correct approach to media inquiries about medico-legal cases — a practical skill the SDL's clinical pearl addresses with three specific sentences.
Tests understanding that pressure from senior colleagues does not override the duty to document accurately in MLCs — a core professional resilience principle.
